title: Skill gaps: Assisted equality can hide learning divides
desc: Separates immediate performance from underlying competence, interaction skill and durable unassisted learning.

kps.k: AI can narrow assisted-performance gaps without equalizing underlying skills; the distributional effect depends on the task and outcome measured.
kps.d: The cluster distinguishes producing better work with AI from acquiring competence that persists without it. In Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, lower-scoring participants improved performance by 43%, versus 17% for higher scorers. In Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps?, a randomized business-task experiment with 1,174 adults reduced the education-based score gap from 0.548 to 0.139 standard deviations—about three quarters—although the residual gap was not statistically significant. These findings concern specific assisted tasks, not equalization of fundamental abilities or economy-wide inequality. Education, baseline performance and AI interaction competence also measure different dimensions of advantage.

qs.q: In the control group without AI, higher-education participants outperform lower-education participants by 0.548 standard deviations; with AI, this gap falls to 0.139 standard deviations, closing about three- quarters of the initial gap.
qs.a: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Learning and discretionary use can instead reward stronger users, challenging a universal equalization claim.
kps.d: Hou, Chen and Tan’s IELTS-coaching experiment with 13,806 students improved writing performance and increased independent practice by 24.9%, but higher baseline proficiency predicted larger gains. They propose that learning requires prior knowledge to absorb feedback, whereas task completion can substitute AI output for missing competence; the experiment does not separately establish that mechanism. The Kenya entrepreneurial experiment reports an overall null alongside subgroup point estimates equivalent to roughly 8% lower profits or revenue among low performers and 15% higher outcomes among high performers. The supplied excerpt provides no uncertainty measures for those estimates. Its authors identify discretion over whether, how and on which tasks to use AI as a possible explanation, not a demonstrated cause of the contrast with constrained experiments.

qs.q: For score gain, the interaction between AI and Baseline Score is positive and statistically significant (β = 0.031, p < 0.01).
qs.a: Does AI Equalize or Amplify? Evidence from Two Field Experiments in AI-powered Learning · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Table A12 shows that our negative point estimate among low performers is equivalent to an approximately 8% drop in profits or revenue among low performers, while our positive point estimate among high performers is equivalent to an approximately 15% increase in profits or revenue.
qs.a: The Uneven Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya · Academia · 2026

kps.k: AI interaction competence may create a new performance divide that conventional academic measures miss.
kps.d: Anand and Idan’s Texas A&M self-study experiment—the same working paper represented by two title variants—found higher mean exam scores with LLM access, 0.56 versus 0.48. Treatment gains varied significantly with AI Interaction Competence: purposeful prompting, output filtering and verification, and iterative application of human judgment. GPA and prior-knowledge interactions were insignificant; novices benefited especially when interaction competence was high. This supports the authors’ proposed shift in the basis of advantage, but insignificant academic interactions do not establish that conventional inequalities disappeared. The study used 179 predominantly undergraduate participants and measured short-term learning rather than workplace output. Completer-only analysis, acknowledged attrition bias favoring the LLM group and inconsistent descriptions of how interaction competence was measured qualify the inference.

qs.q: The average post-intervention exam score among LLM participants was M = .56, SD = .26, compared to M = .48, SD = .23 in the baseline group.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

qs.q: In interaction analysis, the coefficient on the (Treatment × AIC) term was positive and significant (p < 0.05).
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Assisted success does not reliably translate into unassisted learning, and the evidence includes both harm and modest carry-over.
kps.d: How AI Impacts Skill Formation reports reduced acquisition of a new Python-library skill and no significant overall efficiency gain. In the high-school mathematics study, both AI treatments narrowed grade dispersion during assisted practice, but neither produced a significant dispersion effect on unassisted exams; GPT Base students performed worse than controls, while GPT Tutor students did not outperform them. Conversely, the education-gap business experiment found no subsequent average harm and a 0.171-standard-deviation immediate follow-up gain for lower-education participants. Its between-group difference in follow-up treatment effects was insignificant, and the authors explicitly distinguish immediate carry-over from durable learning. These results do not support a blanket claim that AI either harms or strengthens skill formation.

qs.q: 7     Discussion Our main finding is that using AI to complete tasks that require a new skill (i.e., knowledge of a new Python library) reduces skill formation.
qs.a: How AI Impacts Skill Formation · Academia · 2026

qs.q: However, we find no significant effect on HHI for the unassisted exam—i.e., the reduction in the skill gap does not persist when access to AI is removed.
qs.a: Generative AI Without Guardrails Can Harm Learning: Evidence from High School Mathematics · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Cognitive engagement and output integration offer plausible explanations, but most interaction-pattern evidence remains observational.
kps.d: In the programming trial, users who sought conceptual help or explanations achieved higher quiz scores than users with low-scoring interaction patterns; participants were not shown to have been randomly assigned to those behaviors. Exploratory business-task analyses similarly linked stronger follow-up performance to intensive assistance combined with sustained engagement, and described more structured prompting and integration among higher-education users. Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes formalizes a related mechanism in which unequal ability to evaluate AI output changes effort choices and produces long-run skill polarization. That polarization is a theoretical result, not an observed longitudinal outcome. The model’s discussion also limits productivity gains by task suitability and AI reliability, citing external evidence of errors and slowdowns when assistance is unreliable.

qs.q: The high scorers only asked AI conceptual questions instead of code generation or asked for explanations to accompany generated code; these usage patterns demonstrate a high level of cognitive engagement.
qs.a: How AI Impacts Skill Formation · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Consistent with this interpretation, when we divide treated participants into four mutually exclusive groups based on levels of AI assistance and engagement with the task, we find that intensive AI assistance predicts strong task performance even when engagement is low, but follow-up performance is substantially higher only when intensive AI assistance is combined with high engagement with the task.
qs.a: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Targeted instruction and structured guidance can improve outcomes; access or additional exposure alone may not.
kps.d: Training for Technology randomized 164 Hong Kong law students across no access, access alone and access plus application-specific instruction. Access alone produced no significant score improvement; trained students reported greater use and scored nearly one fine grade above the access-only group. This is evidence about mock contract-law examinations, not practicing lawyers or autonomous legal work. Anand and Idan’s conceptual roadmaps raised novice scores from 0.38 to 0.45 and reduced dispersion, although the mean improvement and differential benefit for low-competence users were only weakly significant. An extra mandatory study hour produced no significant gain. In the IELTS study’s second experiment, information disclosure and feedback improved learning and independent practice without increasing total AI usage. Together, these findings motivate investment in application-specific instruction and learning-oriented process design, while leaving broader workplace effects untested.

qs.q: Our experiment took the form of a mock examination administered to 164 law undergraduate (LLB) and graduate (JD) students enrolled in a core module in contract law at the University of Hong Kong.
qs.a: Training for Technology: Adoption and Productive Use of Generative AI in Legal Analysis · Academia · 2026

qs.q: The average post-intervention exam score among scaffolded novices was M = .45, SD = .14, compared to M = .38, SD = .22 in the baseline LLM group, with a weakly significant difference (p > .05, p < .10).
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human-AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Adoption, enthusiasm and perceived success are inadequate substitutes for measuring performance and retained competence.
kps.d: Anand and Idan found only a modest correlation between AI preference and interaction competence, with both enthusiastic weak users and skilled users who preferred other resources. Mathematics students overestimated their relative examination performance under both AI treatments. These findings qualify claims based on satisfaction or adoption alone. The practical implication is to assess assisted quality, time costs, independent practice and unassisted performance separately, rather than treating higher usage or better-looking outputs as proof of learning. Recommendations to preserve cognitive engagement and invest in human–AI collaboration address this distinction; predictions about long-term professional development or labor-market inequality extend beyond the supplied experiments.

qs.q: However, the correlation between preference and ability was only small to moderate (r = 0.26), suggesting that the alignment between preference and actual competence was incomplete.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

qs.q: While students in the GPT Base arm performed worse on the exam (relative to the control arm), they did not perceive that they performed worse or learned less.
qs.a: Generative AI Without Guardrails Can Harm Learning: Evidence from High School Mathematics · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources accept the proposition’s central distinction between AI-assisted performance and underlying or durable competence, and materially develop it through randomized experiments, field studies and a theoretical model. Their common reasoning is that distributional effects depend on what is measured: AI can compress gaps when generated output helps complete a bounded task, yet fail to preserve that compression once assistance is removed, or amplify differences when users must learn, evaluate, integrate and internalize information. Several sources identify prior knowledge, AI interaction competence, cognitive engagement and discretion over use as possible moderators; targeted instruction, feedback and conceptual scaffolding emerge as concrete responses, whereas access, enthusiasm, usage volume or additional exposure alone are unreliable indicators of learning. Material variation remains. Some experiments find larger assisted gains for initially weaker or less-educated participants, while learning and entrepreneurial studies report larger gains—or more favorable point estimates—for stronger participants. Evidence on unassisted outcomes ranges from reduced skill formation and no persistent gap reduction to modest immediate carry-over, which is explicitly not durable learning. Mechanistic confidence also varies: training effects are experimentally tested, but interaction-pattern evidence is generally observational, absorptive capacity is an interpretation, discretion is exploratory, and long-run skill polarization is modeled rather than longitudinally observed. These differences refine rather than reject the proposition and do not justify a blanket claim that AI either equalizes or widens skill gaps.

qs.q: AI may act as an equalizer when the output is the endpoint, but it may act as an amplifier when learning and skill acquisition are the endpoint.
qs.a: Does AI Equalize or Amplify? Evidence from Two Field Experiments in AI-powered Learning · Academia · 2026

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source supports the proposition’s central distinction by showing that GPT-4 narrowed assisted-performance gaps: both initially higher- and lower-scoring participants improved, but the lower-scoring half gained substantially more. This is evidence of task-level equalization under AI assistance, not of equal underlying competence, retained learning, or unassisted performance. The source therefore supports the proposition without establishing its broader claims about learning divides, interaction competence, or durable skill formation. Because only one curated source is supplied for this period, there is no basis for identifying cross-source prevalence or material internal variation; the main qualification is the limited outcome measured—performance on assisted experimental tasks.

qs.q: When comparing the two groups, though, we see the bottom- half-skill performers exhibited the most substantial surge in performance, 43%, compared to the top-half-skill subjects, 17%.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that narrower performance gaps under AI assistance do not necessarily indicate equalized underlying competence or durable learning. In high-school mathematics, both AI treatments reduced grade dispersion during assisted practice, but the reduction disappeared on the unassisted exam. The same study also found that students’ perceptions were more favorable than their actual exam results, reinforcing the proposition that perceived success and assisted output are inadequate measures of retained competence. Internal variation lies mainly between the two treatments: unguarded GPT Base was associated with worse exam performance than the control, whereas GPT Tutor did not outperform the control; neither result supports durable equalization. The source reports limited evidence of heterogeneous effects across preregistered student characteristics, but this does not establish equal effects across students. Its evidentiary scope is confined to a particular educational setting and should not be generalized to workplace adoption at scale.

qs.q: Both GPT Base and GPT Tutor reduced grade dispersion in the assisted practice sessions, matching prior findings that generative AI assistance reduces the “skill gap” by providing the largest benefits for the weakest students ( 7 – 9 ).

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources accept the proposition’s core distinction between AI-assisted performance and underlying or durable competence, and materially develop it with evidence about when gaps narrow, widen or shift to a new dimension. Across the sources, the common explanation is that outcomes depend on what is measured and how AI is used: constrained task execution can let AI substitute for missing expertise and narrow education-based performance gaps, whereas skill acquisition and discretionary use require users to interpret, verify and integrate outputs, potentially rewarding prior proficiency, AI literacy or AI Interaction Competence. The period’s sources also add concrete design implications: targeted legal-analysis training, conceptual roadmaps, tailored scaffolding, disclosure and feedback can improve outcomes, while access, greater usage or additional time alone may not.

Material variation remains. A randomized business-task study finds substantial assisted equalization and modest immediate unassisted carry-over, but explicitly does not establish durable learning. By contrast, a randomized programming study finds reduced new-skill formation, and the IELTS field experiments find larger learning gains among stronger baseline students. The Kenya entrepreneurship experiment reports an overall null with adverse point estimates for low performers and positive ones for high performers, but does not provide uncertainty measures in the supplied excerpt and treats discretion as an exploratory explanation. The theoretical productivity model projects long-run skill polarization from unequal output-evaluation ability rather than observing it longitudinally. The Anand–Idan working paper, represented twice under title variants and therefore not two independent studies, shifts attention from conventional academic advantage to interaction competence; its scaffolding result is suggestive but weakly significant and qualified by attrition and measurement inconsistencies. Several studies use students, short-term tests or exploratory interaction-pattern analyses, limiting claims about durable workplace effects. Thus, the period strengthens and extends the proposition without supporting a universal claim that AI either equalizes or amplifies skill gaps.
